title: Japan Launches New Agency to Deal with Disasters
paragraphs: Japan has launched a new national agency dedicated to preventing and responding to natural disasters, in an effort to make one of the world's most disaster-prone countries better prepared for future catastrophes.

The National Disaster Management Agency officially opened on Monday, November 2. It was created by separating the disaster management bureau from the Cabinet Office, and it employs more than 350 people. The agency will oversee disaster preparedness, emergency response and reconstruction. The legislation establishing it was passed by Japan's parliament in July.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi heads the agency, while Goshi Hosono, the reconstruction minister, will manage it as the newly appointed minister for disaster management. Addressing the agency's staff, Takaichi said that although natural disasters cannot be prevented, the damage they cause can be reduced through preparation.

The agency was not established in response to any specific expected disaster. Rather, it reflects long-standing doubts about whether Japan could cope with a crisis on the scale of the March 2011 earthquake and tsunami, which killed nearly 19,800 people and triggered the Fukushima nuclear disaster.

Government estimates of future disasters are alarming. A megaquake along the Nankai Trough, off Japan's Pacific coast, could kill about 298,000 people and force 6.5 million people to evacuate. A major earthquake directly beneath Tokyo could kill around 18,000 people, while an eruption of Mount Fuji could affect 790,000 people and disrupt transportation and power supplies.

On its first day, the agency issued an "emergency request" urging residents to prepare. Hosono asked people to check whether their homes could withstand earthquakes, secure their furniture, review evacuation procedures, and store enough water and portable toilets for at least three days. The minister also urged people to think about it for themselves and take action.

The agency also aims to improve conditions at evacuation centers by providing clean portable toilets, kitchens for hot meals, bathing facilities and cardboard beds. Local preparation remains a concern, however. According to Hosono, fewer than half of municipal officials have received disaster training in the past five years, and only 15% of municipalities have evacuation plans for older residents and people with disabilities.
